newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Africa sets out on long path to common market dream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Africa sets out on long path to common market dream.

text.p: African economic union is still a far-off dream but the continent's leaders say they are getting the regional building blocks in place.
Several years of good growth after decades of turmoil have allowed them to take their first timid steps towards what many analysts still consider an impracticable idea.
At June's Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit in Zimbabwe, leaders held the first meeting of the African Economic Community (AEC), 17 years after the plan was hatched.
The aim is bold -- to create an African common market for the 54 countries on the continent, but the timetable is a bit more sober -- to achieve it by 2030.
The AEC is supposed to merge existing regional economic groupings, on a poor continent still plagued by conflict, into a single organisation along the lines of the European Union.

"In the 1980s some countries were socialist and policy divided us. For the first time now Africa is pursuing a common economic policy and market reforms have been embraced," said economist Kenneth Kotelo of the Africa Institute in Pretoria.
"But I don't see a single economic community materialising by 2030. You would need to have the regional economic forums functioning first but at the moment they are not."
REGIONAL BLOCS SEEN AS WAY FORWARD
More than half a dozen such groups exist, with differing aims and largely limited success.
"In these institutions lies the embryonic form of community Africa seeks to achieve via political and economic integration," says Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe, current OAU chairman.

In the past it has been cheaper and easier for most African countries, whose economies are still based largely on raw materials and commodities, to trade with their old colonial masters than with their neighbours. This is what they want to change.

African growth has risen from less than one percent in 1992 to over 5.5 percent last year, an upward trend expected to continue. But population growth, at around three percent a year, is still a burden on a continent of a billion people.
Liberalisation and privatisation, led by Uganda and Zambia, have yet to be matched by a boost in foreign investment despite considerable inflows from Asia, led by Malaysia.

"Now that African economies are beginning to grow, basing themselves on private enterprise, we must think of one additional factor -- the size of the market," said President Yoweri Museveni, who has turned Uganda into an economic model.
SOUTHERN AFRICA IS BRIGHTEST HOPE
The brightest star is the southern region, where the end of apartheid in 1994 has brought Africa's long-isolated powerhouse, South Africa, into the fold.
Its membership of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) turned what had been a self-help group for the black "Frontline states" into Africa's strongest economic bloc.
This has fired intra-African trade but also raised fears that smaller economies, already suffering from South Africa's industrial muscle, might not withstand unchecked free trade.

Other groups, like the Maghreb Union, the Nigerian-led Economic Organisation of West African States or the six-nation Central African Customs and Economic Union, are trying to progress but some, paralysed by feuding, exist on paper only.

The Francophone-dominated West African Economic and Monetary Union gives its eight members a single currency and central bank, a coherence the EU can still only dream of but which has been kept alive by French assistance.
They have agreed to cut tariffs on industrial goods within the zone by 60 percent, ahead of eliminating them completely.
Analysts say North Africa, cut off by the Sahara and looking north instead to closer ties with the EU, is the area least committed to pan-African free trade.
With such unevenness between national economies and regional groups, many analysts share Kotelo's scepticism that they will ever fuse easily into a single common market.
SADC EXPANSION ON THE CARDS
In the nearer term, one likely development is that the SADC, imperfect but still the most effective economic forum, will increase its predominance and expand northwards.

It has 12 members, covering the continent south of Kenya and the old Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, whose economies grew an average 6.6 percent last year and who aim for a common market by 2005.
"We have set out on the path to a single regional market in the knowledge that it is no easy path," President Nelson Mandela told a World Economic Forum conference in May.
The SADC has Africa's greatest disparity in gross national product, from South Africa's $3,160 a head to Mozambique's $80.

Its leaders have suggested that Congo, now rid of dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, should join along with Kenya and Uganda, effectively killing off the 20-member Common Market for Southern and Eastern Africa (COMESA) which has failed to make headway.
Analysts think the SADC's growth would probably stop there, with no practical benefit from trying to move west or into the Horn of Africa.
"Expansion of SADC is likely to exacerbate tensions between the Francophone states and so-called Anglophone Africa," said Greg Mills of South Africa's Institute of International Affairs.
Any growth will strain the organisation and leave it with the headache of what to do with turbulent Burundi and Rwanda, which would be encircled if all three candidates joined.
Kenya and Uganda may concentrate instead on reviving the East African Community.
CONFLICT STILL HAMPERS PROGRESS
Instability across Africa, from Sierra Leone to Somalia and from Algeria to the Great Lakes, is still a high hurdle to any economic integration.
It is peace, as well as South Africa's relative power, that has helped turn southern Africa around, and even there Angola's three-year-old peace process is fraying at the edges.
Sceptics question how any fledgling regional economic community could bring in turbulent states and survive.

But African visionaries hope regional blocs could actually cement peace, as the EU did for postwar Western Europe, by weakening arbitrary but seemingly immutable colonial-era borders and the ethnic frictions they have caused.
